claim: HVC is a cortical region in zebra finch that generates sequences underlying the temporal progression of the song.
source: Here we examined the circuit anatomy of zebra finch HVC, a cortical region that generates sequences underlying the temporal progression of the song.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of HVC.

claim: HVC(RA) neurons control song timing.
source: We combined serial block-face electron microscopy with light microscopy to determine the cell types targeted by HVC(RA) neurons, which control song timing.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Close to their soma, HVC(RA) axons almost exclusively targeted inhibitory interneurons.
source: Close to their soma, axons almost exclusively targeted inhibitory interneurons, consistent with what had been found with electrical recordings from pairs of cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by EM data presented in the results.

claim: Far from the soma, HVC(RA) axon targets were mostly other excitatory neurons.
source: Conversely, far from the soma the targets were mostly other excitatory neurons, about half of these being other HVC(RA) cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by EM data in the results.

claim: About half of the excitatory targets far from the soma are other HVC(RA) cells.
source: Conversely, far from the soma the targets were mostly other excitatory neurons, about half of these being other HVC(RA) cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the abstract and supported by EM data.

claim: Neural sequences that pace the song are generated by global synaptic chains in HVC embedded within local inhibitory networks.
source: Both observations are consistent with the notion that the neural sequences that pace the song are generated by global synaptic chains in HVC embedded within local inhibitory networks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings presented in the abstract.

claim: Neural sequences are central to many models of circuit function.
source: Neural sequences are central to many models of circuit function (Diesmann et al., 1999; Jin et al., 2007; Gibb et al., 2009; Fiete et al., 2010; Mostafa and Indiveri, 2014; Cannon et al., 2015a; Rajan et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Neurons often fire sequentially during specific behaviors.
source: neurons often fire sequentially during specific behaviors (Hahnloser et al., 2002; Peters et al., 2014; Mello et al., 2015) or cognitive states (Pastalkova et al., 2008; Harvey et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: The network properties that underlie sequential neural firing are poorly understood.
source: but the network properties that underlie such dynamics are poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: HVC is central to generating the neuronal activity necessary to coordinate activation of vocal muscles during the zebra finch courtship song.
source: Here we explore the synaptic connections within the zebra finch HVC, which is central to generating the neuronal activity necessary to coordinate activation of vocal muscles during the highly reproducible courtship song (Nottebohm et al., 1976; Vu et al., 1994; Aronov et al., 2008; Long and Fee, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Song progression is paced by HVC(RA) neurons.
source: Song progression is paced by HVC(RA) neurons, which project to the primary downstream target area, known as the robust nucleus of the arcopallium (RA) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: HVC(RA) neurons project to the robust nucleus of the arcopallium (RA).
source: Song progression is paced by HVC(RA) neurons, which project to the primary downstream target area, known as the robust nucleus of the arcopallium (RA) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This anatomical fact is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: During the song, an HVC(RA) neuron is either silent or active in the form of a burst of action potentials that occurs at a single precise and cell-specific time.
source: During the song, an HVC(RA) neuron is either silent or active in the form of a burst of action potentials that occurs at a single precise and cell-specific time (Hahnloser et al., 2002; Kozhevnikov and Fee, 2007; Long et al., 2010; Vallentin and Long, 2015).
evidence: This statement about HVC(RA) neuron activity is supported by multiple citations.

claim: At any moment, about 200 HVC(RA) pacer neurons are active and can drive the appropriate motor activity.
source: At any moment, it is estimated that about 200 of these 'pacer' neurons are active and can drive the appropriate motor activity (Fee et al., 2004)
evidence: This estimate is supported by a citation.

claim: HVC(RA) neurons are connected with high probability (>0.50) to nearby inhibitory interneurons.
source: which at the same time showed that HVC(RA) neurons are connected with high probability (>0.50) to nearby inhibitory interneurons (Mooney and Prather, 2005; Kosche et al., 2015).
evidence: This finding from paired recordings is supported by citations.

claim: Direct connections between HVC(RA) neurons are only rarely seen with paired intracellular recordings.
source: Such connections are, however, only rarely seen with paired intracellular recordings, which at the same time showed that HVC(RA) neurons are connected with high probability (>0.50) to nearby inhibitory interneurons (Mooney and Prather, 2005; Kosche et al., 2015).
evidence: This observation from paired recordings is supported by citations.

claim: Paired recordings may fail to correctly estimate the connection rate between excitatory cells due to severing of axons during slice preparation.
source: There are, however, a number of reasons paired recordings may fail to correctly estimate the connection rate between excitatory cells, among them the severing of axons during slice preparation (Stepanyants et al., 2009)
evidence: This potential limitation is supported by a citation.

claim: Paired recordings may fail to correctly estimate the connection rate between excitatory cells due to oversampling of closely spaced neurons.
source: There are, however, a number of reasons paired recordings may fail to correctly estimate the connection rate between excitatory cells, among them the severing of axons during slice preparation (Stepanyants et al., 2009) and an oversampling of closely spaced neurons (Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: This potential limitation is supported by a citation.

claim: HVC(RA) dendrites are compact, with 95.0 ± 2.0% (SEM) of the dendritic path found within 100 µm of the soma.
source: In agreement with other observations (Dutar et al., 1998; Mooney, 2000; Kosche et al., 2015), we found that HVC(RA) dendrites were compact, with 95.0 ± 2.0% (SEM) of the dendritic path found within 100 µm of the soma (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from LM reconstructions, shown in Figure 1e and consistent with prior work.

claim: HVC(RA) axon collaterals are lined with synaptic boutons throughout.
source: In contrast, the axon collaterals, which were lined with synaptic boutons throughout (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b), ramified across HVC.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: For each HVC(RA) cell (n = 15), the dendrite was entirely (100%) confined to HVC.
source: For each cell (n = 15), the dendrite was entirely (100%) confined to HVC, while the axon (with the exception of the branch projecting to RA) was also largely restricted to the boundaries of HVC (97% on average).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from LM reconstructions of 15 cells.

claim: The HVC(RA) axon (with the exception of the branch projecting to RA) was largely restricted to the boundaries of HVC (97% on average).
source: For each cell (n = 15), the dendrite was entirely (100%) confined to HVC, while the axon (with the exception of the branch projecting to RA) was also largely restricted to the boundaries of HVC (97% on average).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from LM reconstructions of 15 cells.

claim: The SBEM data set had an overall size of 166 × 166 × 77 µm³.
source: To quantify the prevalence of different types of synaptic inputs onto the dendrite of HVC(RA) cells, we next acquired a SBEM data set (166 × 166 × 77 µm3 overall size, comprising 15104 × 15104×2661 voxels, each 11 × 11 × 29 nm3 in size) from the central part of HVC (Figure 1f, Figure 1—figure supplement 1f–j, Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a description of the EM data acquisition parameters.

claim: Within the SBEM volume, 34 somata were positively identified as HVC(RA) neurons by the presence of a BDA-derived electron density.
source: Within this volume, 34 somata were positively identified as HVC(RA) neurons by the presence of a BDA-derived electron density (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is a count of labeled neurons in the EM volume.

claim: 34 labeled HVC(RA) somata is approximately 14% of the expected value of HVC(RA) somata (240 ± 28, SEM).
source: This number is approximately 14% of the expected value of HVC(RA) somata (240 ± 28, SEM), given that there are about 40,000 ± 3800 (SEM) HVC(RA) cells (Wang et al., 2002) and the total HVC volume is 0.35 ± 0.024 mm3 (n = 14, SEM).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the observed count and published estimates.

claim: There are about 40,000 ± 3800 (SEM) HVC(RA) cells.
source: given that there are about 40,000 ± 3800 (SEM) HVC(RA) cells (Wang et al., 2002)
evidence: This estimate is from a cited publication.

claim: The total HVC volume is 0.35 ± 0.024 mm³ (n = 14, SEM).
source: and the total HVC volume is 0.35 ± 0.024 mm3 (n = 14, SEM).
evidence: This is a measurement from the current study.

claim: For 12 of the 34 labeled HVC(RA) neurons, the dendrite was manually reconstructed (skeletonized) as far as possible.
source: For 12 of the 34 labeled HVC(RA) neurons, we manually reconstructed (skeletonized) (Helmstaedter et al., 2011) the dendrite as far as possible.
evidence: This describes the reconstruction procedure for a subset of neurons.

claim: EM-based dendritic reconstructions ranged in dendritic path length from 642 µm to 1956 µm (1290 ± 469 µm, mean ± SD).
source: These reconstructions ranged in dendritic path length from 642 µm to 1956 µm (1290 ± 469 µm, mean ± SD) compared with complete LM-based reconstructions (1438 µm to 4819 µm, mean ± SD: 3187 ± 997 µm).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the EM reconstruction data.

claim: Complete LM-based dendritic reconstructions ranged from 1438 µm to 4819 µm (mean ± SD: 3187 ± 997 µm).
source: These reconstructions ranged in dendritic path length from 642 µm to 1956 µm (1290 ± 469 µm, mean ± SD) compared with complete LM-based reconstructions (1438 µm to 4819 µm, mean ± SD: 3187 ± 997 µm).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the LM reconstruction data.

claim: ~70% (174 out of 248) of dendritic branches reached the boundary of the EM data set and were thus incomplete.
source: Although ~70% (174 out of 248) of dendritic branches reached the boundary of the EM data set and were thus incomplete, 74 branches were completely reconstructed, including their most distal inputs
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of reconstruction completeness.

claim: 74 dendritic branches were completely reconstructed, including their most distal inputs.
source: Although ~70% (174 out of 248) of dendritic branches reached the boundary of the EM data set and were thus incomplete, 74 branches were completely reconstructed, including their most distal inputs
evidence: This is a count of complete reconstructions.

claim: For one HVC(RA) cell, 396 (39.5%) synapses were asymmetric and thus presumably excitatory, and 607 (60.5%) were symmetric (inhibitory).
source: We started by classifying for one cell all (1,003) incoming synapses (Figure 1g–h) by visually inspecting their ultrastructural details (Gray, 1959; Colonnier, 1968) (Videos 4 and 5). We found that 396 (39.5%) synapses were asymmetric and thus presumably excitatory, and 607 (60.5%) were symmetric (inhibitory) cases.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from synapse classification in EM, shown in Figure 1g-h.

claim: In 19 out of 20 randomly selected test cases, a second expert independently came to the same synapse classification conclusion.
source: Our synapse classification is reliable: in 19 out of 20 randomly selected test cases, a second expert independently came to the same conclusion
evidence: This is a validation of the synapse classification method.

claim: In a test set of 8 HVC(RA), 11 HVC(X), and 31 interneuron synapses where the neuron type was known, all synapses were correctly classified by an expert unaware of the cell type.
source: and in another set of test cases (8 HVC(RA), 11 HVC(X), and 31 interneuron synapses), where the neuron type was known based on somatic and dendritic morphology (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), all synapses were correctly classified by an expert unaware of the cell type.
evidence: This is another validation of the synapse classification method.

claim: The dominance of inhibitory synaptic inputs was consistently observed for HVC(RA) cells.
source: The dominance of inhibitory synaptic inputs was consistently observed for HVC(RA) cells: when we applied our synapse classification procedure to 97 short dendritic stretches (first and third quartile of stretch length: 13.3 µm and 21.6 µm) randomly selected from eight of the other skeletonized HVC(RA) cells, we found that across neurons the average ratio between excitatory and inhibitory synapses was statistically indistinguishable (p=0.36, one-way ANOVA) from that found in the completely analyzed neuron.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of synapse counts across multiple cells.

claim: Inhibitory synapses were significantly enriched near the soma (68 ± 4% of all synapses at most 40 µm from the soma are inhibitory compared to 57 ± 2%, for synapses beyond that distance, mean ± SEM, p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
source: Inhibitory synapses were significantly enriched near the soma (68 ± 4% of all synapses at most 40 µm from the soma are inhibitory compared to 57 ± 2%, for synapses beyond that distance, mean ± SEM, p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Figure 1i)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical significance, shown in Figure 1i.

claim: The enrichment of inhibitory synapses near the soma is an observation also made in cortical neurons.
source: Inhibitory synapses were significantly enriched near the soma (68 ± 4% of all synapses at most 40 µm from the soma are inhibitory compared to 57 ± 2%, for synapses beyond that distance, mean ± SEM, p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Figure 1i), an observation also made in cortical neurons (Anderson et al., 1994).
evidence: This comparison to cortical neurons is supported by a citation.

claim: Dendritic synapse density for asymmetric synapses is 0.25 ± 0.02 µm⁻¹ (mean ± SEM).
source: To estimate the number of excitatory and inhibitory synapses that a single HVC(RA) neuron receives on average, we first calculated dendritic synapse densities for all nine analyzed cells separately for asymmetric (0.25 ± 0.02 µm−1, mean ± SEM) and for symmetric synapses (0.36 ± 0.02 µm−1).
evidence: This is a calculated density from EM data.

claim: Dendritic synapse density for symmetric synapses is 0.36 ± 0.02 µm⁻¹ (mean ± SEM).
source: To estimate the number of excitatory and inhibitory synapses that a single HVC(RA) neuron receives on average, we first calculated dendritic synapse densities for all nine analyzed cells separately for asymmetric (0.25 ± 0.02 µm−1, mean ± SEM) and for symmetric synapses (0.36 ± 0.02 µm−1).
evidence: This is a calculated density from EM data.

claim: On average, 59% (1144 ± 429, mean ± SD) of all synapses onto HVC(RA) dendrites are symmetric.
source: Thus, on average well above half of all synapses onto HVC(RA) dendrites are symmetric (59%, 1144 ± 429, mean ± SD) and only 41% are asymmetric (786 ± 311)
evidence: This is a calculated estimate based on synapse densities and dendritic path length.

claim: On average, 41% (786 ± 311, mean ± SD) of all synapses onto HVC(RA) dendrites are asymmetric.
source: Thus, on average well above half of all synapses onto HVC(RA) dendrites are symmetric (59%, 1144 ± 429, mean ± SD) and only 41% are asymmetric (786 ± 311)
evidence: This is a calculated estimate based on synapse densities and dendritic path length.

claim: The dominance of inhibitory inputs in HVC(RA) neurons stands in stark contrast to mammalian cortical neurons where inhibitory synapses are typically at most 20% of the total.
source: — a surprising dominance of inhibitory inputs that stands in stark contrast to mammalian cortical neurons (Beaulieu et al., 1992; Peters, 2002; Kasthuri et al., 2015), where the inhibitory synapses are typically found to be at most 20% of the total.
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to studies of mammalian cortex.

claim: 44 homotypic synapses between HVC(RA) cells were found.
source: We found 44 such homotypic synapses between HVC(RA) cells (see Materials and methods)
evidence: This is a count of double-labeled synapses in the EM data.

claim: Homotypic HVC(RA) synapses comprise only about 1% among an estimated total of 3817 ± 926 (SD) incoming excitatory synapses.
source: but they comprise only about 1% among an estimated total of 3817 ± 926 (SD) incoming excitatory synapses.
evidence: This is a calculated proportion based on the count of double-labeled synapses.

claim: The median size of homotypic HVC(RA) synapses is 0.21 µm².
source: Their median size (0.21 µm2) and size variation (first and third quartile: 0.10 µm2 and 0.48 µm2), were statistically indistinguishable from those for all asymmetric synapses (0.17 µm2; first and third quartile: 0.08 µm2 and 0.39 µm2, p>0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Figure 1k).
evidence: This is a measurement from EM data, shown in Figure 1k.

claim: The size of homotypic HVC(RA) synapses is statistically indistinguishable from all asymmetric synapses (p>0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
source: Their median size (0.21 µm2) and size variation (first and third quartile: 0.10 µm2 and 0.48 µm2), were statistically indistinguishable from those for all asymmetric synapses (0.17 µm2; first and third quartile: 0.08 µm2 and 0.39 µm2, p>0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Figure 1k).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of synapse sizes.

claim: BDA labeled only a small fraction (1/7th) of all HVC(RA) cells in the EM data set.
source: However, BDA labeled only a small fraction (1/7th) of all HVC(RA) cells in our data set (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a)
evidence: This is an observation about labeling efficiency, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4a.

claim: The axonal labeling probability is 7.6 ± 1.6% (SEM).
source: The axonal labeling probability of 7.6 ± 1.6% (SEM, see Materials and methods)
evidence: This is a calculated estimate based on measurements in the EM volume.

claim: Homotypic HVC(RA) synapses constitute ~15 ± 4% (SEM) of all excitatory synapses onto HVC(RA) neurons.
source: The axonal labeling probability of 7.6 ± 1.6% (SEM, see Materials and methods) in turn implies that the homotypic HVC(RA) synapses constitute ~15 ± 4% (SEM) of all excitatory synapses onto HVC(RA) neurons.
evidence: This is an estimate corrected for labeling efficiency.

claim: The three main cell types found in HVC are inhibitory interneurons, HVC(RA) neurons, and HVC(X) neurons.
source: The three main cell types found in HVC (Dutar et al., 1998; Kubota and Taniguchi, 1998; Mooney, 2000) are easily distinguished in LM
evidence: This classification is supported by citations.

claim: Inhibitory interneurons have smooth dendrites with a nearly complete lack of spines.
source: Inhibitory interneurons have smooth dendrites with a nearly complete lack of spines (Mooney, 2000; Wild et al., 2005)
evidence: This morphological characteristic is supported by citations.

claim: Spine density is 0.01 ± 0.01 spines/µm (mean ± SD) for interneurons.
source: Dendrites were largely aspinous (0.01 ± 0.01 spines/µm, mean ± SD) for interneurons, densely covered with spines (0.70 ± 0.13 spines/µm) for HVC(X) cells and less so (0.21 ± 0.07 spines/µm) for HVC(RA) neurons.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from LM data.

claim: Spine density is 0.70 ± 0.13 spines/µm (mean ± SD) for HVC(X) cells.
source: Dendrites were largely aspinous (0.01 ± 0.01 spines/µm, mean ± SD) for interneurons, densely covered with spines (0.70 ± 0.13 spines/µm) for HVC(X) cells and less so (0.21 ± 0.07 spines/µm) for HVC(RA) neurons.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from LM data.

claim: Spine density is 0.21 ± 0.07 spines/µm (mean ± SD) for HVC(RA) neurons.
source: Dendrites were largely aspinous (0.01 ± 0.01 spines/µm, mean ± SD) for interneurons, densely covered with spines (0.70 ± 0.13 spines/µm) for HVC(X) cells and less so (0.21 ± 0.07 spines/µm) for HVC(RA) neurons.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from LM data.

claim: The spine density metric correctly classified 17 out of 18 BDA-labeled HVC(RA) dendrites in EM.
source: This spine density metric correctly classified 17 out of 18 BDA-labeled HVC(RA) dendrites in EM as well as 11 inhibitory neurons that had been classified using other morphological characteristics (symmetric synapses and a large soma diameter, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a validation of the spine density classification method.

claim: Three BDA-stained axons that each emerged from labeled somata in the SBEM dataset had path lengths of 1.37, 0.88, and 0.72 mm.
source: When we examined three BDA-stained axons that each emerged from labeled somata in the SBEM dataset (path lengths: 1.37, 0.88, and 0.72 mm)
evidence: This is a measurement of axon path lengths in the EM volume.

claim: Of 121 connections from three proximal BDA-stained axons, 115 terminated on dendrites of inhibitory cells but only six onto excitatory cells, four of which being other HVC(RA) cells.
source: we found that of 121 connections, 115 terminated on dendrites of inhibitory cells but only six onto excitatory cells, four of which being other HVC(RA) cells (e.g., Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a count of synaptic targets from EM data, shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The high connectivity between HVC(RA) neurons and interneurons agrees with electrical recordings from pairs of cells.
source: This agrees with the high connectivity found for closely spaced HVC(RA)-interneuron pairs by electrical recordings (Kosche et al., 2015)
evidence: This comparison is supported by a citation.

claim: Six orphaned BDA-labeled axon fragments had a path length of 0.56 ± 0.27 mm (mean ± SD).
source: We then examined BDA-labeled axon fragments that were 'orphaned' (n = 6, path length: 0.56 ± 0.27 mm, mean ± SD), i.e., could not be traced back to their soma and were therefore likely farther away from it.
evidence: This is a measurement of orphaned axon path lengths.

claim: Three of the orphaned axon fragments were synaptically connected to one of the labeled dendrites.
source: Three of the fragments were synaptically connected to one of the labeled dendrites and four were partially myelinated.
evidence: This is an observation about the orphaned fragments.

claim: Four of the orphaned axon fragments were partially myelinated.
source: Three of the fragments were synaptically connected to one of the labeled dendrites and four were partially myelinated.
evidence: This is an observation about the orphaned fragments.

claim: The prevalence of synapses onto excitatory neurons increased 13-fold for orphaned fragments compared to attached axons, from 5.0% (6 out of 121) to 64.6% (263 out of 407).
source: We discovered that the prevalence of synapses onto excitatory neurons, and onto other HVC(RA) cells in particular, was much larger for orphaned fragments than for attached axons; increases were 13-fold (HVC(RA)-E), from 5.0% (6 out of 121) to 64.6% (263 out of 407)
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of synaptic targets between proximal and distal axons.

claim: The prevalence of synapses onto other HVC(RA) cells increased 11-fold for orphaned fragments compared to attached axons, from 3.3% (4 out of 121) to 36.8% (150 out of 407).
source: and 11-fold (HVC(RA)-HVC(RA)), from 3.3% (4 out of 121) to 36.8% (150 out of 407) (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison shown in Figure 3a.

claim: HVC(RA) dendrites were often connected by more than one synapse to a labeled axon (17 doubles, 3 triple, and 1 quintuple among 127 analyzed pairs).
source: HVC(RA) dendrites were often connected by more than one synapse to a labeled axon (17 doubles, 3 triple, and 1 quintuple among 127 analyzed pairs).
evidence: This is a count of multi-synapse connections.

claim: The connection probability between HVC(RA) cells found in electrophysiological recordings is 0.7%.
source: This would also be consistent with the low connection probability of 0.7% between HVC(RA) cells found in electrophysiological recordings (Kosche et al., 2015)
evidence: This value is from a cited publication.

claim: In electrophysiological recordings, recorded somata are usually less than 200 µm apart.
source: where the recorded somata are usually less than 200 µm apart (Mooney and Prather, 2005; Jiang et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a characteristic of paired recording experiments, supported by citations.

claim: 56 ± 14% (SD) of the axon collaterals' path lies farther than 200 µm from the soma.
source: while, as our LM reconstructions show, 56 ± 14% (SD) of the axon collaterals' path lies farther than 200 µm from the soma
evidence: This is a measurement from LM reconstructions.

claim: Branching becomes less frequent as the distance from the soma increases.
source: It is apparent from our LM reconstructions that branching becomes less frequent as the distance from the soma increases (Figure 3b,c).
evidence: This observation is shown in Figure 3b,c.

claim: HVC(RA) axons in the SBEM data set that were connected to a cell body had 12.4 ± 3.7 (mean ± SD) branch points/mm.
source: Consistent with this, HVC(RA) axons in the SBEM data set that were connected to a cell body were much more highly branched (12.4 ± 3.7, mean ± SD, branch points/mm, Figure 2e) than most orphaned axon fragments, with an average of only 4.0 ± 4.3 (mean ± SD) branch points/mm.
evidence: This is a measurement from EM data, shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Orphaned axon fragments had an average of 4.0 ± 4.3 (mean ± SD) branch points/mm.
source: Consistent with this, HVC(RA) axons in the SBEM data set that were connected to a cell body were much more highly branched (12.4 ± 3.7, mean ± SD, branch points/mm, Figure 2e) than most orphaned axon fragments, with an average of only 4.0 ± 4.3 (mean ± SD) branch points/mm.
evidence: This is a measurement from EM data.

claim: A synapse is much more likely to be connected to another HVC(RA) cell or to a HVC(X) neuron rather than to an inhibitory neuron if the synapse is farther away from the soma.
source: We found that a synapse was much more likely to be connected to another HVC(RA) cell or to a HVC(X) neuron rather than to an inhibitory neuron if the synapse was farther away from the soma (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from the distance estimation analysis, shown in Figure 3d.

claim: One orphaned axon with unusually high branch density (11.4 branch points/mm) made the majority of its connections (52 of 83, 63%) onto interneurons.
source: One of the orphaned axons (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) showed an unusually high branch density (11.4 branch points/mm), suggesting a location close to the soma (16th to 84th percentile: 35.8 to 72.3 µm and also made the majority of its connections (52 of 83, 63%) onto interneurons
evidence: This is an observation about a specific orphaned axon, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: There are approximately 1111 ± 513 (SD) outgoing synapses inside HVC for each HVC(RA) neuron.
source: Since there are approximately 1111 ± 513 (SD) outgoing synapses inside HVC for each HVC(RA) neuron (given an axon path length of 14.7 mm and a total synapse density of 75.4 synapses/mm)
evidence: This is a calculated estimate based on axon path length and synapse density.

claim: Each HVC(RA) neuron is expected to have about ~191 ± 88 (SD) homotypic synapses.
source: we expect about ~191 ± 88 (SD) homotypic synapses per cell (on average, incoming and outgoing homotypic synapse have to be equal in number)
evidence: This is a calculated estimate based on the fraction of homotypic synapses observed.

claim: Homotypic synapses comprise about a quarter (24 ± 4%, SEM) of all incoming excitatory synapses.
source: comprising about a quarter (24 ± 4%, SEM) of all incoming excitatory synapses
evidence: This is a calculated proportion based on the estimate of homotypic synapses.

claim: Homotypic synapses comprise nearly half of all outgoing excitatory contacts.
source: and nearly half of all outgoing excitatory contacts.
evidence: This is a calculated proportion based on the axonal perspective.

claim: DiI injection into HVC heavily labeled the upstream nuclei NIf and Uva.
source: To independently confirm the number of RA(HVC) cells, we injected the fluorescent tracer DiI (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA) into HVC, which heavily labeled the upstream nuclei NIf and Uva (Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is an observation from a retrograde tracing experiment, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: DiI injection into HVC yielded only a small number of labeled somata in RA (125, 163, and 171, respectively, in three birds).
source: but yielded only a small number of labeled somata in RA (125, 163, and 171, respectively, in three birds), approximately one for every 200 HVC(RA) neurons on average.
evidence: This is a count from the retrograde tracing experiment.

claim: There is approximately one RA(HVC) neuron for every 200 HVC(RA) neurons on average.
source: but yielded only a small number of labeled somata in RA (125, 163, and 171, respectively, in three birds), approximately one for every 200 HVC(RA) neurons on average.
evidence: This is a calculated ratio from the retrograde tracing data.

claim: The synaptic architecture in HVC contains a density of connections between HVC(RA) neurons that might be sufficient to support a synaptic-chain model.
source: We have shown that the synaptic architecture in HVC contains a density of connections between HVC(RA) neurons that might be sufficient to support a synaptic-chain model
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: 25% of excitatory inputs to HVC(RA) neurons are homotypic.
source: While we estimate that 25% of excitatory inputs to HVC(RA) neurons are homotypic
evidence: This is a summary of the estimate from the results.

claim: The sources of the remaining 75% of excitatory synapses onto HVC(RA) neurons are unknown.
source: While we estimate that 25% of excitatory inputs to HVC(RA) neurons are homotypic, the sources of the remaining synapses are unknown.
evidence: This is implied by the statement that 25% are homotypic and the sources of the remaining are unknown.

claim: Removal of NIf does not disrupt the song.
source: since removal of NIf does not disrupt the song (Cardin et al., 2005).
evidence: This finding is supported by a citation.

claim: With around 200 homotypic inputs per HVC(RA) cell, the probability to be connected to any one of around 40,000 HVC(RA) neurons can be at most 0.5%.
source: The reason is that with the around 200 homotypic inputs per cell, the probability to be connected to any one of around 40,000 HVC(RA) neurons can be at most 0.5%.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the number of homotypic inputs and total HVC(RA) neurons.

claim: HVC(RA) neurons preferentially form distal connections.
source: One potential difficulty stems from our finding that HVC(RA) neurons preferentially form distal connections
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding from the results.

claim: The timing circuitry in HVC is distributed.
source: indicating that the timing circuitry in HVC is distributed
evidence: This is an inference from the finding of distal connections.

claim: Complete reconstruction of the timing circuitry in HVC requires a large EM volume (as much as 500 million µm³, compared to 2 million µm³ in the current volume).
source: and therefore requires a large EM volume (as much as 500 million µm3, compared to 2 million µm3 in our volume) for its complete reconstruction.
evidence: This is an estimate of the volume needed for complete reconstruction.

claim: Connections near the soma are often onto inhibitory neurons.
source: Our finding that connections near the soma are often onto inhibitory neurons suggests that inhibition plays an important role in sequence generation
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding from the results.

claim: Inhibition plays an important role in sequence generation in HVC.
source: Our finding that connections near the soma are often onto inhibitory neurons suggests that inhibition plays an important role in sequence generation
evidence: This is an inference from the finding about proximal inhibitory connections.

claim: The large overall fraction of inhibitory inputs supports the idea that inhibition plays an important role in sequence generation.
source: which is further supported by the large overall fraction of inhibitory inputs.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding about the dominance of inhibitory synapses.

claim: Inhibitory connections could decorrelate excitatory activity in space and time.
source: One function of those inhibitory connections could be to decorrelate excitatory activity in space and time
evidence: This is a proposed function based on the findings.

claim: Nearby HVC(RA) neurons are rarely connected and thus unable to drive each other.
source: Not only are nearby HVC(RA) neurons rarely connected and thus unable to drive each other
evidence: This is an inference from the findings about proximal connectivity.

claim: Strong reciprocal inhibition creates a winner-take-all effect in HVC.
source: but even when driven by a common input, only the cell(s) with the strongest input(s) will continue to fire in the face of the winner-take-all effect due to the strong reciprocal inhibition (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism illustrated in Figure 3h.

claim: Winner-take-all behavior in HVC may help to prevent local clusters of activity.
source: In HVC, it may help to prevent local clusters of activity, which could lead to leakage across different chains passing through adjacent excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is a proposed function of the winner-take-all mechanism.

claim: Local inhibition may improve temporal precision by sharpening burst timing through recurrent inhibition.
source: An altogether different role for local inhibition may be the improvement of temporal precision by sharpening burst timing through recurrent inhibition (Hahnloser et al., 2002; Long et al., 2010; Cannon et al., 2015a).
evidence: This proposed role is supported by citations.

claim: Inhibition may have a central role in shaping the distance dependency of postsynaptic targets during circuit development without the need for molecular cues.
source: Inhibition may, furthermore, have a central role in shaping the distance dependency of postsynaptic targets during circuit development without the need for molecular cues (de Wit and Ghosh, 2016).
evidence: This proposed developmental role is supported by a citation.

claim: The observed architecture may arise from an initial pattern following Peters' rule that is then refined as interneurons prevent co-activation of nearby excitatory cells.
source: Instead, the architecture we observed may arise naturally from a pattern that initially follows Peters' rule (Braitenberg and Schüz, 1998), which predicts synaptic connections between cell types with intermingled axonal and dendritic arbors (Rees et al., 2017), but is then refined as the interneurons increasingly prevent the co-activation of nearby excitatory cells, thereby destabilizing connections between them while leaving more distant connections intact.
evidence: This is a proposed developmental mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Preferentially distal connectivity would favor more widely distributed synaptic chains.
source: Such a preferentially distal connectivity would also favor more widely distributed synaptic chains
evidence: This is an inference from the finding of distal connectivity.

claim: Widely distributed synaptic chains could rely more on axonal propagation delays for sequence timing.
source: which could have the added benefit of relying more on axonal propagation delays for sequence timing (Budd et al., 2010).
evidence: This proposed benefit is supported by a citation.

claim: The observed synaptic architecture shows resemblance with local inhibitory/excitatory networks linked by long-range excitatory/excitatory connections (coupled winner-take-all modules).
source: Overall, the observed synaptic architecture shows some resemblance with local inhibitory/excitatory networks linked by long-range excitatory/excitatory connections (coupled winner-take-all modules) that have been shown to make computational models of cortical sequence generation more robust (Binas et al., 2014; Mostafa and Indiveri, 2014).
evidence: This comparison to computational models is supported by citations.

claim: Adult male zebra finches were used in this study.
source: We used adult (>90 days post hatch) male zebra finches that were obtained from an outside breeder
evidence: This describes the animals used in the study.

claim: 200 nL of either Fluoro-Ruby (50 mg/mL) or BDA (100 mg/mL) was injected into RA.
source: We injected 200 nL of either Fluoro-Ruby (50 mg/mL) or BDA (100 mg/mL) into RA of anesthetized (1–3% isoflurane in oxygen) zebra finches
evidence: This describes the injection procedure.

claim: RA was targeted using stereotaxic coordinates (2.30 mm lateral and 1.85 mm posterior from the midsagittal sinus).
source: RA was targeted using stereotaxic coordinates (2.30 mm lateral and 1.85 mm posterior from the midsagittal sinus)
evidence: This describes the targeting method.

claim: The SBEM voxel size was 11 × 11 × 29 nm³.
source: We performed serial block-face electron microscopy (Denk and Horstmann, 2004) at 11 × 11 × 29 nm voxel size
evidence: This describes the imaging parameters.

claim: SBEM imaging was performed at 2 kV landing energy.
source: at a dose of 10.3 electrons/nm2, 2 kV landing energy
evidence: This describes the imaging parameters.
